title: Paris, 1900–1913
subtitle: From Satie’s first Gymnopédie to The Rite of Spring

hero.caption: Claude Monet, Impression, soleil levant, 1872, Musée Marmottan Monet. An orange sun over the boats in the harbour at Le Havre, in mist.

intro: Satie set a melody over two quiet piano chords; twenty-five years later, Stravinsky wrote a stamping dance for orchestra. Between them came Debussy’s sea and clouds, Ravel’s birds and plucked strings, and the Ballets Russes in Paris.

stations.title: Satie’s first Gymnopédie
stations.text: Satie played the piano at the Chat Noir cabaret, then at the Auberge du Clou, where he met Debussy. His first Gymnopédie, written in 1888, opens with a bass note on the first beat and a soft chord on the second. G and D alternate below. The melody enters after four bars, and its long F♯ is held over the changing chords. Later, a low E is held while the harmony moves beneath it. The first ending closes on D major before the music starts again.

cues.text: The melody enters after four bars; its held F♯ sounds above the alternating G and D bass notes.
The melody holds E while three different chords pass beneath it.
The closing phrase falls from G to F♯; two full chords close the first half in D major.

stations.title: Gongs in Paris; bells at the piano
stations.text: At the 1889 Paris Exposition, Debussy heard Javanese gamelan, with gongs sounding beneath quicker instrumental patterns. In the Revue musicale S.I.M. in 1913, he wrote that its counterpoint made Palestrina’s seem like “child’s play”. His Pagodes of 1903 had already brought gong-like bass notes to the piano. Here Marcelle Meyer plays La cathédrale engloutie, published in 1910. Bare fifths rise slowly, with long spaces between them in which the notes ring. The left hand then begins rolling figures beneath the ascending chords, which represent the cathedral of Breton legend rising from the sea.

cues.text: Marcelle Meyer plays La cathédrale engloutie, in which bare fifths rise in the piano.
The left hand begins rolling in triplets beneath the rising chords as the cathedral emerges.

stations.title: Debussy’s Nuages and Monet’s harbour

art.caption: Claude Monet, Impression, soleil levant, 1872. An orange sun and dark boats against the mist over the harbour at Le Havre.

stations.text: Paris first heard Nuages in December 1900. In the middle of the piece, flute and harp share a five-note melody over soft held strings. The cor anglais then returns with its earlier narrow phrase. Monet painted Impression, soleil levant from a hotel window in Le Havre in 1872. Dark boats are placed close to the viewer; the orange sun and its reflection stand out against the mist. Farther back, cranes and masts are barely visible in the morning haze.

cues.text: Flute and harp play a melody built on five notes over quiet held chords in the strings.
The cor anglais plays its earlier phrase again as the flute-and-harp tune dies away.
The returning phrases grow shorter.

stations.title: Ravel’s writing for strings
stations.text: Ravel finished his String Quartet in April 1903 and dedicated it to his teacher, Fauré. The scherzo opens pizzicato, with both violins, viola and cello plucking their notes. A bowed melody then enters in a long phrase over the continuing pizzicato. Debussy took an interest in how the four parts sat together. Writing to Ravel before the première in March 1904, he suggested a small change to the playing, that the viola could be a little quieter.

cues.text: Two violins, viola and cello play the dance pizzicato in short, separate notes.
The bowed melody is played in long notes above quick plucked notes.

stations.title: Hokusai’s wave on the cover of Debussy’s score

art.file: File:Katsushika Hokusai - Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji- The Great Wave Off the Coast of Kanagawa - Google Art Project.jpg
art.caption: Katsushika Hokusai, The Great Wave off Kanagawa, c. 1830–32, colour woodblock print. The wave arches over small boats, with Mount Fuji beyond.

stations.text: The United States Air Force Band plays the opening of La Mer in Lawrence Odom’s concert-band transcription. A low B is held beneath the opening; short phrases enter above it, one at a time. Later, groups of two and three notes cross one another. When Durand published the score in 1905, its cover carried an adapted detail of Hokusai’s wave. In the complete print, narrow boats lie under the curling crest, and Mount Fuji stands far behind them.

cues.text: Odom’s concert-band transcription opens over a held low B, with short phrases above it.
The low notes are held while shorter phrases begin to move above them.
After the slow opening, the music moves faster; short calls enter over a running accompaniment.
Groups of two notes cross groups of three in the quiet movement.

stations.title: Ravel’s Oiseaux tristes
stations.text: Ravel described the birds of Oiseaux tristes as lost in a dark forest during the hottest hours of summer. The piano begins high and alone, with a repeated B♭ and a short flourish. Beneath the next calls, the left hand moves in threes while the right hand divides its beat in two. A louder call is followed by a quiet answer. Ravel dedicated the piece to Ricardo Viñes, who first played Miroirs at the Salle Érard on 6 January 1906. When the opening call returns in D minor, held chords sound beneath it.

cues.text: A high B♭ repeats softly, then opens into a small flourish; the left hand is silent.
The left hand plays in threes beneath the right hand’s twos and the bird’s call.
A loud call is answered quietly, at a distance, while the lower notes continue to turn.
The opening call returns in D minor over soft held chords.

stations.title: Karsavina as the bird

art.caption: Léon Bakst, costume design for the Ballets Russes production of The Firebird, 1910.

stations.text: On 25 June 1910, Tamara Karsavina danced The Firebird at the Paris Opéra, with choreography by Michel Fokine for Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes. In the Infernal Dance, the bird forces Kashchei and his creatures to dance. The United States Marine Band plays Thomas Knox’s arrangement for concert band. Short figures cut across the pulse, and the accents are displaced. Bakst’s costume design shows the bird on paper, before a dancer wore it. A longer melody then extends across the beat, while Kashchei remains under her spell.

cues.text: The Marine Band plays Thomas Knox’s arrangement of Kashchei’s forced dance, which is built from short phrases.
Sharp accents fall across the steady pulse.
After the clipped opening phrases, a longer melody runs across the beat.

stations.title: The opening bassoon solo
stations.text: On 29 May 1913, Pierre Monteux conducted the première of The Rite of Spring at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées. Nijinsky had choreographed the ballet for Diaghilev’s company. The music begins with a bassoon high in its range, playing a melody drawn from a Lithuanian folk-song collection. Other wind instruments enter around it, each with a separate line. In this recording Stravinsky conducts the Columbia Symphony Orchestra, in January 1960. Near the end of the introduction the wind parts thin out and the opening bassoon tune returns, briefly exposed, before the stamping begins.

cues.text: A bassoon plays a winding melody high in its range; the other wind instruments enter one by one.
Separate wind phrases overlap, cross and interrupt one another around the opening melody.
The wind calls thin out before the dance, leaving space around the bassoon.

stations.title: Augurs of Spring: the repeated chord
stations.text: The strings repeat the same chord at the opening of Augurs of Spring, F♭ major against an E♭ dominant seventh. Horns play selected attacks harder. The opening bars keep a steady 2/4 while the accents shift, with unaccented strokes between them. In a letter to Nicholas Roerich on 26 September 1911, Stravinsky described an old woman in squirrel fur running in front of the dancers, stopping and interrupting their rhythm. He had her in mind while composing this dance. Around the repeated chord, shorter phrases pass across the orchestra, and the horns enter again.

cues.text: The strings repeat their crowded chord; horns pick out certain strokes with extra force.
The dance opens in 2/4, with quiet strokes filling the uneven gaps between the accents.
The dance grows louder around its recurring figures, then grows quieter again.
A repeated tread holds beneath the shorter phrases.
